## Ezekiel 41 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter falls into four main sections: (1) the interior of the temple — the Holy Place and Most Holy Place (vv. 1–4); (2) the wall and side chambers (vv. 5–11); (3) the western building and the separate place (vv. 12–15a); (4) interior finish, ornaments, and furnishings (vv. 15b–26).

A major interpretive divide runs through all the commentaries: whether Ezekiel describes a **literal, future temple** to be built in Jerusalem (a view prominent among dispensational and some Baptist teachers, e.g., David Guzik / Enduring Word), or whether the vision is **symbolic/ideal** — presenting the perfect dwelling of God with His people in terms the exiles could grasp (the dominant Reformed, Lutheran, and older Anglican view — e.g., Ligonier, Ellicott, Matthew Henry). Catholic tradition (Haydock) holds a both/and view: the vision partly relates to the material temple but ultimately to the Church of Christ. John Gill (Baptist) interprets the temple entirely as the Gospel church.

---

### v. 1 — The Outer Sanctuary (Holy Place) Entrance

**"Then the man brought me into the outer sanctuary and measured the side pillars to be six cubits wide on each side."**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** "The temple" (הַהֵיכָל) here means the nave or Holy Place specifically, not the whole complex. The measuring began from the east wall. The side pillars (doorposts) were six cubits broad — thicker than those of the porch, which were only five cubits (Ezekiel 40:48). The phrase "which was the breadth of the tabernacle" (KJV) likely means these measurements related to the whole breadth of the covered edifice, here called "tabernacle" to connect it to the wilderness sanctuary. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Ellicott:** The six cubits refer to the thickness of the side walls. An apparent discrepancy exists between "six cubits" here and "five cubits" in v. 2 for the sides of the door; Ellicott explains that v. 1 measures thickness (depth) of the wall, while v. 2 measures width of the door opening. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **John Gill (Baptist):** The temple represents "the Gospel church state in general," especially in the latter-day glory. The posts six cubits broad each — "this was the frontispiece of the door of the palace of the King of kings." He notes the breadth of the two posts together (12 cubits) matched the entire breadth of Moses' tabernacle, showing how much larger the Gospel church is than the old synagogue. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-41.html]

- **Enduring Word (Charismatic/Pentecostal-leaning):** Because Ezekiel was a priest, he could enter the Holy Place with his guide. The detailed measurements anchor the vision in physical reality — "a real room with actual spatial dimensions." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-41/]

- **Matthew Henry (Puritan/Reformed):** The very doorposts were as wide as the whole breadth of Moses' tabernacle (12 cubits). This shows that "wide is the gate which leads into the church, the ceremonial law, that wall of partition which had so much straitened the gate, being taken down." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/41.htm]

---

### v. 2 — Dimensions of the Holy Place

**"The width of the entrance was ten cubits… He also measured the length of the outer sanctuary to be forty cubits, and the width to be twenty cubits."**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The door opening was ten cubits (narrower than the porch door of eleven cubits, making it more conspicuous). The interior dimensions — forty cubits long by twenty wide — exactly match Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:2, 17). The entire frontage calculation: 6+6 (pillars) + 5+5 (side walls) + 10 (door opening) = 32 cubits. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Gill:** The door was twice as broad as Solomon's temple door (which was only five cubits). This wider entrance suggests greater access to God under the Gospel. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-41.html]

- **Enduring Word:** These are exactly the dimensions of Solomon's temple — further evidence this describes a real, material building. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-41/]

---

### v. 3 — The Inner Sanctuary Entrance

**"And he went into the inner sanctuary and measured the side pillars at the entrance to be two cubits wide. The entrance was six cubits wide, and the walls on each side were seven cubits wide."**

- **Pulpit Commentary & Preacher's Homiletical Commentary:** It is significant that "he went in" — not "he brought me in." Ezekiel, though a priest, could not enter the Most Holy Place; only the high priest could, once a year. The measuring-man went in alone and reported the measurements to Ezekiel. The post was two cubits; the door six cubits; the breadth of the door seven cubits. This is a difficult verse: some take "six" as height and "seven" as breadth; others understand "six" as the distance between posts and "seven" as the actual door width. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm] [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-41.html]

- **Gill:** The door was two-leaved; each leaf three cubits broad, with a middle post of one cubit making seven cubits total. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-41.html]

- **Enduring Word:** Ezekiel did not follow his guide inside — reinforcing that this is a real room governed by real priestly protocol, not merely a symbol. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-41/]

---

### v. 4 — The Most Holy Place

**"Then he measured the room adjacent to the inner sanctuary to be twenty cubits long and twenty cubits wide. And he said to me, 'This is the Most Holy Place.'"**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The Holy of Holies was an exact square of twenty cubits — identical to Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:20). It lay across the whole breadth of the Holy Place. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Gill:** This square shape "denotes its stability and perfection." It is an emblem of "the most holy and perfect state of the church on earth" — the New Jerusalem church state where nothing defiling enters and Christ Himself dwells. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-41.html]

- **Matthew Henry:** "For the new Jerusalem is exactly square (Rev. 21:16), denoting its stability; for we look for a city that cannot be moved." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary:** The Most Holy Place is so called because in the Tabernacle and Solomon's Temple the Shekinah — the visible manifestation of divine glory — dwelt there. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-41.html]

---

### v. 5 — Temple Wall and Side Chambers

**"Next he measured the wall of the temple to be six cubits thick, and the width of each side room around the temple was four cubits."**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The outer wall was six cubits thick — colossal, matching Eastern architectural norms. Like Solomon's temple, side chambers served as storerooms for priestly garments, temple utensils, and treasures. The chambers were four cubits broad in the clear. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Gill:** The six-cubit wall represents God's strong protection of His church — "salvation will be for walls and bulwarks." The side chambers represent "particular congregated churches" where believers, made priests to God, have communion in holy things. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-41.html]

- **Enduring Word:** "The massiveness of the walls is remarkable; both inside and outside walls are thicker than the width of the rooms" (quoting Block). This is a carefully engineered, strongly built literal structure. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-41/]

---

### vv. 6–7 — The Three Stories of Chambers

**"The side rooms were arranged one above another in three levels of thirty rooms each… The side rooms… widened at each successive level…"**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The chambers were arranged in three stories of thirty each (ninety total) — matching Josephus' description of Solomon's temple. The chambers were not fastened into the temple wall itself but rested on ledges or rebatements. An "enlarging" occurred as one went up: the second story was wider than the first, and the third wider than the second, because the wall thickness decreased by one cubit at each level (from six to five to four cubits), creating ledges for the beams. A winding staircase (as in Solomon's temple, 1 Kings 6:8) provided access. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Gill:** The enlargement of chambers as they ascend "may denote the enlargement of the church of Christ, as it comes nearer the heavenly state." The lower storey (narrowest) = the present church age; the middle = the latter-day glory; the uppermost = the New Jerusalem church state, "very large, and next to heaven." The winding stairs signify "the various afflictions and tribulations, trials and exercises, in which the Lord leads his people." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-41.html]

- **Matthew Henry:** "The higher we build up ourselves in our most holy faith the more should our hearts, those living temples, be enlarged." God builds high but also firmly — the timber had hold, "but not in the wall of the house," so one part was not weakened to strengthen another. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Enduring Word:** The side rooms "were probably used to store gifts and tithes and various temple vessels (cf. Nehemiah 13:5, 9, 12)" (quoting Wright). The description is admittedly "difficult to follow" but consistent with a literal building. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-41/]

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** Notes that accuracy of measurement, according to Hebrew concepts, was "a necessary ingredient of perfection." Nothing was done by caprice or at random (citing Exodus 25:9-10; Hebrews 8:5). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-41.html]

---

### vv. 8–9 — Raised Base and Outer Wall

**"I saw that the temple had a raised base all around it… a full rod, six long cubits… The outer wall of the side rooms was five cubits thick…"**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The temple stood on a raised basement or platform — like many ancient temple buildings. The "six great cubits" likely refers to the height of the foundation. The outer wall of the side chambers was five cubits thick. The "place that was left" (v. 9) is obscure: Keil and Kliefoth view it as a walkway of five cubits outside the chambers; Ewald places it between the temple wall and the side chambers as a light passage. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Gill:** The "full reed of six great cubits" refers to the foundation of the uppermost storey (which was six cubits). These foundations signify Christ, "ministerially laid by his twelve apostles," the only sure foundation. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-41.html]

- **Haydock (Catholic):** "That which was left" means the space between chambers, placed to manifest greater respect for God. Josephus describes a dividing wall three cubits high, five cubits from the temple. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-41.html]

---

### vv. 10–11 — Open Area and Chamber Doors

**"…the open area between the side rooms… and the outer chambers was twenty cubits wide… The side rooms opened into this area, with one entrance on the north and another on the south. The open area was five cubits wide all around."**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The twenty-cubit free space lay between the outer wall of the side chambers and the cells of the inner court. The chambers opened onto a corridor five cubits broad. Verses 10–11 together allow calculation of the entire temple breadth as 100 cubits. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Gill:** The doors signify "the free entrance of men into the churches of Christ in the latter day, whose gates shall be opened to let in the righteous nation." The five-cubit void space represents the communion of churches. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-41.html]

---

### v. 12 — The Western Building

**"Now the building that faced the temple courtyard on the west was seventy cubits wide, and the wall of the building was five cubits thick all around, with a length of ninety cubits."**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The "separate place" (gizrah, from a root meaning "to cut off") was a marked-off area behind the temple on the west, devoted to less sacred purposes. Kliefoth suggests it was for receiving refuse, sweepings, and everything "separated or rejected" during holy service — hence the name. The building was 70 cubits broad, 90 cubits long, with walls 5 cubits thick. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Gill:** This building, near the Most Holy Place, may "design heaven itself, the happiness and glory of the saints treasured up and reserved there." The 70 cubits breadth recalls the 70 years of life's labours before entering eternal rest (following Jerome). The five-cubit wall answers to "the vast gulf fixed between the godly in heaven, and the wicked in hell" (Luke 16:26). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-41.html]

- **Enduring Word:** The western side had no gate; this building stood at its western end. A substantial, real building. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-41/]

- **Matthew Henry:** Perhaps this other building "signified the setting up of a church among the Gentiles not inferior to the Jewish temple, but of quite another nature, and which should soon supersede it." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/41.htm]

---

### vv. 13–14 — Overall Temple Dimensions

**"Then he measured the temple to be a hundred cubits long… The width of the temple courtyard on the east… was a hundred cubits."**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The whole temple complex measured 100 cubits long and 100 cubits broad — a perfect square. The total temple area (including courts) was 500 cubits square. The square shape echoed the Holy of Holies and anticipated the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:16). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Gill:** Breaks down the 100 cubits length thus: east porch wall (6) + porch passage (11) + wall between porch and temple (6) + Holy Place (40) + wall between Holy Place and Most Holy (2) + Most Holy (20) + west wall (6) + chambers at end (4) + outer wall of chambers (5) = 100. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-41.html]

---

### vv. 15–17 — Galleries and Interior Paneling

**"Next he measured the length of the building facing the temple courtyard at the rear… a hundred cubits. The outer sanctuary, the inner sanctuary, and the porticoes… were overlaid with wood on all sides… paneled from the ground to the windows, and the windows were covered."**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Verses 15–17 give a summary with new details. The galleries (attikim) were passages or porticos running along both north and south sides, supported by pillars or wall-ledges. The thresholds, narrow windows, and galleries were covered with wood wainscoting from floor to windows. The windows were "covered" — either protected by lattice-work (Ewald, Plumptre) or wainscoted as well (Currey). Everything proceeded "by measure" — nothing random. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** The windows "were covered from the view below, perhaps with lattice work." Accuracy of measurement was considered "a necessary ingredient of perfection." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-41.html]

---

### vv. 18–20 — Cherubim and Palm Trees

**"…were alternating carved cherubim and palm trees. Each cherub had two faces: the face of a man… and the face of a young lion…"**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** As in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:29), the wainscoting was adorned with alternating cherubim and palm trees. Only two of the cherub's four faces could be shown on a flat surface: the man's face (symbolizing rational creation) toward one palm tree, and the young lion's face (symbolizing irrational creation) toward the other. This ornamentation ran "from the ground unto above the door." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary:** "Cherubim a symbol of Divine life; palm-trees of life in general." The cherubim "indicate that the house is dedicated to the God of the whole terrestrial creation; not to a national god of limited power." The faces looking toward the palms indicate "all creation, animate and inanimate, is a whole — a harmonious work of the creative power of God." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-41.html]

- **Enduring Word:** "In these figures aspirations of life and prosperity (palm) and security (cherubim) coalesce" (quoting Block). The two faces — man and young lion — "suggested perfect realisation of created life, and its perfect exercise in kingly dominion" (quoting G. Campbell Morgan). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-41/]

- **Matthew Henry:** The cherubim "represent the angels, who have more than the wisdom of a man and the courage of a lion; and in both they have an eye to the palms of victory and triumph which are set before them." In church assemblies, angels are specially present (1 Corinthians 11:10). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/41.htm]

---

### v. 21 — The Doorframes

**"The outer sanctuary had a rectangular doorframe, and the doorframe of the sanctuary was similar."**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The doorposts of the temple were squared (not round like pillars). The "appearance of the one as the appearance of the other" is variously interpreted: (a) the sanctuary door had square posts like the temple door (Kliefoth, Keil); (b) the appearance matched what Ezekiel had formerly described (Plumptre); (c) the appearance in this vision matched other visions and the actual temple (Currey). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Matthew Henry:** In the Tabernacle and Solomon's temple the door of the Most Holy Place was narrower than that of the temple. Here it was equally broad — "for in gospel-times the way into the holiest of all is made more manifest than it was under the Old Testament (Heb. 9:8)." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/41.htm]

---

### v. 22 — The Wooden Altar / Table

**"There was an altar of wood three cubits high and two cubits square… And the man told me, 'This is the table that is before the LORD.'"**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** This is the altar of incense (Exodus 30:1), distinct from the altar of burnt offering in the outer court. In the tabernacle and Solomon's temple it was wood overlaid with gold; here it is described simply as wood. Plumptre suggests Ezekiel "did not contemplate an abundance of gold as likely to be the outcome of the scant offerings of an impoverished people." Its dimensions (3 cubits high × 2 × 2) are larger than the tabernacle altar (2 × 1 × 1). The "corners" are likely the horns. "Table" and "altar" are convertible terms — it stands before the Lord as a place of fellowship. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Enduring Word:** This is far too small for animal sacrifice (just over 5 feet high and under 3.5 feet long). It is the altar of incense — "a representation of the prayers of God's people." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-41/]

- **Matthew Henry:** No mention of gold overlay — "it intimates that the incense to be offered in the gospel-temple shall be purely spiritual, and the fire spiritual, which will not consume an altar of wood. Therefore this altar is called a table." The great sacrifice having been offered, what remains is "to feast upon the sacrifice at the Lord's table." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Gill:** This is the altar of incense before the Lord. "Table" is used because at it the Lord takes delight in His people "as at a feast." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-41.html]

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary:** "Table and altar are convertible terms. It stood in front of the vail, and is therefore said to be before the Lord." Not to be confused with the eight tables outside at the north gate for burnt offerings (Ezekiel 40:49). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-41.html]

---

### vv. 23–24 — Double Doors

**"Both the outer sanctuary and the inner sanctuary had double doors, and each door had two swinging panels…"**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The doors of both the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place were double, each door consisting of two folding leaves. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Matthew Henry:** Both the temple and the sanctuary each had its own two-leaved, folding door. In the Old Testament the way into the Holiest was not yet manifest; under the Gospel the door into the Holiest is wider. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Enduring Word:** The doors were of folding construction with two panels hinged together. Notes that John Trapp's spiritualizing reading (that the doors speak of baptism and the Lord's Supper) is speculative and "undermines the straightforward reading." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-41/]

---

### vv. 25–26 — Carvings on Doors and Canopies

**"Cherubim and palm trees like those on the walls were carved on the doors of the outer sanctuary, and there was a wooden canopy outside… There were beveled windows and palm trees on the sidewalls of the portico. The side rooms of the temple also had canopies."**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The doors were carved with the same cherubim and palm tree motifs as the walls. A wooden canopy (or "covering") stood in front of the vestibule outside. Only palm trees — not cherubim — adorned the porch and side chambers, marking them as subordinate to the temple proper. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary:** "The porch and likewise the wings take the character of the subordinate from this, that only palms are figured on them, and not cherubim also." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-41.html]

- **Matthew Henry:** "Thus the living temples are adorned, not with gold, or silver, or costly array, but with the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/41.htm]

- **Enduring Word:** "Once more, the detailed nature of this description only makes sense if Ezekiel described a literal, material temple that will one day stand in Jerusalem." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-41/]

---

## Major Interpretive Differences Among Protestant Traditions

### Literal/Futurist View (Dispensational, some Baptist, Pentecostal/Charismatic)

**David Guzik (Enduring Word):** Insists throughout that the precise dimensions, engineering details, and priestly protocols make sense only if Ezekiel described a "literal, material temple that will one day stand in Jerusalem." Spiritualizing interpretations (like Trapp's reading of the doors as baptism and the Lord's Supper) "undermine the straightforward reading." The side chambers were for storing temple vessels; the walls were "carefully engineered"; the altar is physically distinct from the altar of sacrifice. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-41/]

**Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** Treats the measurements as describing an actual temple structure, with attention to architectural detail, while also drawing typical lessons (e.g., cherubim indicate the building is "dedicated to the God of all creation, not to a national god, of limited powers"). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-41.html]

### Symbolic/Ideal View (Reformed, Lutheran, some Anglican)

**Ligonier Ministries (Reformed):** Explicitly disagrees with the literal future-temple view. Reasons: (1) Ezekiel often uses vivid metaphors; (2) dimensions appear symbolic (multiples of five, perfect cube unlike Solomon's temple); (3) the post-exilic community was never condemned for not building Ezekiel's temple. "God was speaking a language the exiles could understand in order to convince them of His good intentions." The vision points to the progressive revelation culminating in Christ. [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ezekiel-sees-new-temple]

**Ellicott's Commentary (Anglican):** The vision must be prophetic, but "the à priori presumption must be in favour of the latter [ideal/symbolic], since all was seen 'in the visions of God' — an expression which Ezekiel always applies to a symbolic representation rather than to an actual image of things." The second temple was quite unlike Ezekiel's, and the returning exiles made no attempt to follow these plans. If this were meant literally, "it is inconceivable that there should be no allusion to the language of Ezekiel in… Ezra and Nehemiah, and… Haggai." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-41.html]

**Matthew Henry (Puritan/Reformed):** Reads the temple as Christ's body, the Church, and individual believers. The widening upper chambers picture the enlarging of the heart through faith. The wooden altar without gold overlay suggests spiritual worship. The square shape anticipates the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:16). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/41.htm]

### Spiritual/Ecclesiological View (Particular Baptist)

**John Gill:** The entire temple represents "the Gospel church state in general" and especially the latter-day glory. Every measurement and feature has a spiritual referent: the thick walls = God's protection; chambers = particular churches; winding stairs = tribulations leading upward; the western building = heaven itself. The enlarged upper chambers = the church's enlargement as history progresses toward the New Jerusalem. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-41.html]

---

## Other Views

### Catholic Reading

**Haydock's Catholic Bible Commentary:** Following Challoner (Douay-Rheims), this vision "partly had relation to the material temple, which was to be rebuilt: and partly, in a mystical sense, to the spiritual temple of God, the Church of Christ." Because Zerubbabel's temple was meaner than Solomon's while Ezekiel's vision describes something grander, "this prophecy… cannot be understood of it, but of the Church" — citing St. Jerome and St. Augustine (City of God, XVIII.45). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-41.html]

### The Expositor's Bible Commentary (Older critical scholarship)

The fundamental idea is "the literal dwelling of Jehovah in the midst of His people." The temple is "Jehovah's palace, where He manifests His gracious presence." Through the veil of legal institutions, "the prophet saw the day of Christ." The vision symbolises "reconciliation between God and man" and the "sanctification of human life in all its relations through spiritual communion with the Father revealed in our Lord Jesus Christ." Christian interpreters have differed on how the vision is realised, "but on one point at least they are agreed, that through the veil of legal institutions the prophet saw the day of Christ." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-41.html]
